name: Cycloastragenol

lead: Cycloastragenol is the sugar-free form of astragaloside IV, a compound from astragalus root. People take it as an anti-ageing supplement, hoping slower cellular ageing shows up as younger-looking skin and more vitality.

The idea is that it activates telomerase, the enzyme that extends the protective ends of chromosomes, which in turn slows cellular ageing. Cell studies report a moderate rise in telomerase activity and animal models show reduced inflammation. A small human study exists on a related telomerase-activator product, and no trial has measured skin or appearance.

paras: It is taken as a daily oral supplement, usually sold as capsules, often as part of a longevity stack alongside other ageing-focused compounds. Users generally describe it as a long-term routine, with any change expected to build gradually over months.

Human safety data are limited and toxicity data are sparse. Telomerase is active in most cancers, so a theoretical concern exists about activating it. The FTC issued a consent order over ageing-reversal advertising for the branded product TA-65. It is sold as a supplement, not an approved drug.

angle.text: Cycloastragenol is marketed as a telomerase activator: the idea is slower cellular ageing, which users hope shows up as a younger look and more vitality. Support so far comes from cell and animal work.

lead: Cycloastragenol is a tetracyclic triterpenoid obtained from the roots of Astragalus species, notably Astragalus membranaceus. It is the aglycone (sugar-free form) of astragaloside IV, a major saponin of the herb used in traditional Chinese medicine.[1][2][3] It is marketed as a supplement ingredient, including as the active component of the TA-65 brand, on the claim that it activates telomerase, the enzyme that extends the protective ends of chromosomes, with the aim of supporting healthy ageing.[1][4]

The appearance angle is the one that goes with any anti-ageing product: people who take it hope that slowing cellular ageing will show up as younger-looking skin and a more youthful overall appearance. That chain runs through telomerase activation, which has been studied in cultured cells (including skin keratinocytes and fibroblasts) and in mice, and in a handful of human trials that measured immune, telomere and cardiometabolic markers rather than appearance.[5][6][7] A topical product, TA-65 for Skin, was also marketed by the same company.[8]

Wikipedia describes the telomerase-activation claim as not well established: a preliminary study on human T cells reported a moderate increase in telomerase activity, and the clinical significance is uncertain.[1] Most research on the compound is preclinical, covering inflammation, neuroprotection, cardiovascular and cancer models in cells and rodents.[9][10][11][12] No published trial has tested cycloastragenol for facial appearance, skin or hair outcomes in people.

paras: Cycloastragenol has a 9,19-cyclolanostane skeleton with hydroxyl groups at several positions and an epoxy-bridged side chain; it is the aglycone formed when sugars are removed from astragaloside IV.[2] It is poorly soluble in water.[2] It occurs in the roots of Astragalus membranaceus and A. mongholicus, with content varying by origin and growing conditions.[2] Astragaloside IV, the parent glycoside, is converted to cycloastragenol in part by gut-microbial and hepatic metabolism, according to a network-pharmacology study.[3]

Telomeres are repeating DNA sequences at chromosome ends that protect them from damage. Telomerase is the enzyme that adds those repeats, using its own RNA template, and its catalytic protein is called TERT. It is normally active in germ cells and most cancer cells but largely absent from most adult body cells, which lose telomere length as they divide until they reach a senescent state known as the Hayflick limit.[4]

Elizabeth Blackburn and Carol Greider discovered telomerase in 1984, and with Jack Szostak shared the 2009 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine.[4] Wikipedia notes that telomere shortening does not appear to drive ageing in some tissues, that the contribution of telomere length to lifespan remains unresolved, and that telomerase is active in roughly 85 to 90 percent of human tumours; it also notes that mice with elevated telomerase had higher cancer incidence and did not live longer.[4]

According to Wikipedia, Geron patented cycloastragenol, and Telomerase Activation Sciences acquired the rights in early 2013 to develop the TA-65 supplement.[1] Bill Andrews of Sierra Sciences tested TA-65's anti-ageing effects, though Wikipedia flags the reliability of that source.[1] A 2012 lawsuit challenging the company's anti-ageing claims was reported in Nature News, and a UK novel-foods advisory committee received an application to market cycloastragenol.[1]

The US Federal Trade Commission issued a consent order against Telomerase Activation Sciences over advertising that implied TA-65 could reverse ageing and repair DNA damage; the final order was approved on 19 April 2018.[1] Wikipedia also notes that much supporting material comes from manufacturers and that few high-impact peer-reviewed publications exist.[1]

A commercial health-maintenance programme containing TA-65, branded PattonProtocol-1, launched in 2007, and its first-year data were published in 2011 with authors affiliated with Geron.[5] TA-65 is sold as capsules and powder (TA-65MD) and, at the time of the FTC action, also as a topical cream marketed for skin.[8]

Proponents and review articles describe telomerase activation, through signalling such as MAPK/ERK, as the main anti-ageing mechanism.[2][13] Reviews of traditional Chinese medicine anti-ageing ingredients and of plant compounds that target telomeres list cycloastragenol alongside astragaloside IV, resveratrol and ginsenoside Rg1.[7][14] Preclinical studies also report effects on SIRT1 expression in a brain-ischaemia model,[9] suppression of NLRP3 inflammasome activation in endothelium, cardiac tissue and a psoriasis-like skin model in mice,[10][12][15] and enhanced anti-tumour T-cell immunity in a cancer model.[11]

Human data on cycloastragenol itself are limited and largely come from studies of the TA-65 branded product, whose main ingredient is cycloastragenol. A registered trial completed in 2016 with 48 participants examined a telomerase activator in relation to retinal amyloid in Alzheimer disease.[16] No controlled trial of cycloastragenol for appearance or skin ageing has been published.

The first-year report of the PattonProtocol-1 programme, published in 2011 in Rejuvenation Research, was uncontrolled and combined TA-65 with supplements and physician counselling. The authors reported that low nanomolar concentrations moderately activated telomerase in cultured keratinocytes, fibroblasts and immune cells; that the share of senescent CD8+CD28- T cells fell, mostly in people seropositive for cytomegalovirus; that mean telomere length did not increase but the share of very short telomeres fell; and that no adverse events were attributed to the programme.[5]

A double-blind, randomised crossover trial in 40 people with metabolic syndrome, published in 2018 in Current Pharmaceutical Design, gave TA-65 or placebo for 12 weeks each with a washout between. Compared with placebo, TA-65 was associated with higher HDL cholesterol and lower body mass index, waist circumference, LDL/HDL ratio and tumour necrosis factor-alpha.[6] The protocol for a 90-person randomised pilot trial in older adults after acute coronary syndrome, funded by the manufacturer, measured immune-senescence markers, telomere length and endothelial function with TA-65MD versus placebo; the protocol itself reports no results.[17]

Laboratory and animal work includes a 2009 conference abstract reporting that cycloastragenol may moderately raise telomerase activity in human CD4 and CD8 T cells, a 2013 sponsor-funded study of T cells from six participants in which TA-65 activated telomerase in all cultures (Wikipedia says the clinical significance is uncertain), and a 2011 Maria Blasco study in Aging Cell in which TA-65 lengthened short telomeres and improved healthspan measures in mice without raising cancer incidence or extending lifespan.[1] A skin-ageing review of nanotechnology approaches covers anti-ageing actives for the skin in general.[18]

On 21 February 2018 the US Federal Trade Commission announced charges against Telomerase Activation Sciences and its chief executive, Noel Patton. The FTC alleged the company claimed TA-65MD and TA-65 for Skin reverse ageing, that TA-65MD prevents or repairs DNA damage, restores ageing immune systems, increases bone density and lowers cancer risk, and that the skin cream shortened skin recovery time after medical procedures, without competent scientific evidence.[8]

The FTC also alleged that a 2012 television segment was paid advertising presented as independent programming and that endorsers shown as independent users had received free product worth up to $4,000. Under the consent order, the company must substantiate health claims with scientific evidence, may not claim products are clinically proven for the listed functions, must disclose material connections, and had to notify recent direct purchasers.[8]

Wikipedia notes that much supporting material on TA-65 comes from the manufacturer and that few high-impact peer-reviewed publications exist.[1] Reviewers of plant-derived compounds that target telomeres list cycloastragenol among candidates while describing the work as preclinical.[14]

Wikipedia states that toxicity testing is limited and human safety has not been adequately demonstrated.[1] Because abnormal telomerase activity features in most cancers, it raises a theoretical but unproven concern about cancer promotion; the 2011 mouse study cited there found no increase in cancer incidence.[1] The authors of the 2020 trial protocol describe the cancer question as debated, cite earlier studies reporting no adverse events or laboratory toxicity over a year, and note possible interactions with immunosuppressants and effects on blood sugar and blood pressure.[17] Cycloastragenol has also been studied for anti-cancer effects in cell models.[11]

lore.intro: Cycloastragenol is discussed in longevity and anti-ageing circles as a telomerase-activating supplement, and its appearance promise rests on the idea that slower cellular ageing will show in skin and vitality.[1][8]
